World.title: Palestinians told to leave homes in village where Israeli settlers besieged houses
World.content:
About a dozen Palestinian households in a village in the occupied West Bank were told to leave their properties during an Israeli military operation to remove Israeli settlers.

The settlers had besieged residents in three homes in the area since Sunday, cutting off their power and water supplies.

Qusra Mayor, Abdel Azim Wadi, told the BBC that his village had been declared a closed military zone - and Israeli forces were using some of the vacated Palestinian houses as barracks. The Israeli military said the aim was "to protect the residents".

An Israeli spokesman told the BBC the settlers' action was "deplorable" and "unacceptable" and the government would investigate and arrest those responsible.

"The Israeli army is acting against it, and we are investigating it and we will arrest those responsible and we will prosecute them," David Mencer said.

Settlers have been emboldened by the rapid expansion of settlements under the current Israeli government â leading to a dramatic rise in settler violence as they try to drive Palestinians off their land.

All settlements are illegal under international law.

Of the besieged families' three homes in Qusra, which are made up of the Abu Ridi and Hassan families, the residents of two were told to leave on Thursday, they told the BBC. They said those told to leave had since moved into the third house.

Elsewhere in the village, the residents of 11 other houses had also been told to leave by the army.

World.title: Romania shuts only nuclear plant as heat causes huge drop in Danube River level
World.content:
Romania has shut down its only nuclear power station because of extremely low water levels in the Danube river caused by prolonged hot weather affecting much of Europe.

The CernavodÄ plant, where two reactors produce about 20% of Romania's electricity, is not expected to be restarted within the next 10 days.

Earlier this week, authorities tried to increase the water flow to the plant - which uses the Danube for cooling - by sinking barges loaded with rocks in the river.

Neighbouring Hungary has so far avoided a shutdown of its only nuclear plant in Paks, which also uses the Danube. The waters in Europe's second-longest river have fallen to the lowest levels for 30 years in several countries.

The second of the two 706-megawatt reactors at CernavodÄ was disconnected from the Romanian electricity grid just before midday on Thursday.

"We do not foresee a restart within the next 10 days," plant director Romeo Urjan told the AFP news agency.

The first reactor had already been shut down in July.

Until now, CernavodÄ had only been shut down once before in 2003.

The shortfall in power is usually covered by solar and wind during the hot, windy daytimes - but traditional coal- and gas-powered generation will have to be supplemented by imports during the evenings.

Romania also has huge hydropower capacity, although that has been heavily cut by the same low river levels that caused the nuclear shutdown.

In Hungary, Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar warned last month that the Soviet-era Paks, which has four nuclear reactors, could be forced to shut down entirely for the first time.

Plant officials said that levels in the Danube were so low that the suction nozzles used to take in water could not reach it.

World.title: Putin can no longer claim victory in Ukraine, Nobel Peace Prize winner tells BBC
World.content:
What the Kremlin had assumed in 2022 would be a short, successful "military operation" has become the bloodiest conflict in Europe since World War Two.

Yet a confident President Vladimir Putin continues to predict victory for Russia.

"There will never be 'victory'," counters Muratov. "Because what has been going on for nearly five years â no matter how it ends â can no longer be considered a victory.

"It cannot be a victory when two Slavic nations have ripped a million people to shreds. Or more than a million."

"It seems to me that the situation with Ukraine now is this: you can destroy it, but you cannot conquer it. What do I mean by destroy? Continued escalation all the way to the use of a nuclear weapon."

Does he really believe the Kremlin leader would use nuclear weapons in this war?

"All those political experts who say 'Putin thinks this' or 'Putin is scared of that'â¦they're all charlatans," claims Muratov. "It's in the same league as astrology. Nobody knows what's going on in Vladimir Putin's head. And I don't know.

"I see things only as a journalist. I study big data. And since the beginning of the year the need to use nuclear weapons has been mentioned more than 500 times. When wackos say this, I pay no attention. But I've heard it discussed on state TV. And at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum, a state-run event, one of the speakers talked up the use of nuclear weapons as something favourable, something good."

When he announced the mass invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Putin spoke of "ensuring the security of Russia."

"Tell me, has security increased?" Muratov asks. "With Ukrainian drones now attacking warehouses of [Russia's largest online retailer] Wildberries; with the petrol crisis, the disruption to mobile internet, the political prisoners? Has security increased, or not?"

Despite opinion polls registering a fall in Putin's domestic approval ratings, Russia's president â Muratov believes - retains a tight grip on power.

"Sorry, I don't believe all this talk about a split among members of the elite, about secret conspiracies. The country is run by Vladimir Putin. They're frightened of him.

"And this fear is reinforced in every way by his main support base: the Federal Security Service (FSB)."

As critical as he is of his own government, he has few illusions about the West.

"[Putin] knows very well the true value of European leaders. On the one hand they talk to him about human rights. He laughs out loud because, with the other hand, they sign agreements â or used to sign agreements â with Russia on trading oil, gas, diamondsâ¦all that stuff. When they talk to Putin about European values, he truly laughs out loud. He knows the true value of people who preached to him those values."

In Russia Muratov has been designated a "foreign agent", a label often used to punish critics of the Kremlin. "Foreign agents" have limited rights: they're banned from teaching, from taking part in elections; if they sell their flat, they can't access the assets. The label is also designed to stigmatise, to create the sense in society of an enemy within.

Yet the journalist appears reluctant to focus on the pressures he's under, preferring instead to highlight the plight of compatriots in prison.

"What worries me most right now is that no one in the world is interested in the political prisoners who were first to speak out against the land grab in our neighbouring country," Muratov explains.

World.title: Conditions on US aircraft carrier at sea for more than 250 days raise alarms
World.content:
Thousands of US military members who have been living aboard an aircraft carrier for more than 250 days are reportedly contending with food shortages, broken plumbing, exhaustion, and other hardships, leading lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon and putting pressure on the Trump administration over the Iran war.

Military news outlets reported that multiple sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln have considered jumping overboard, as well.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday called reports of poor conditions "completely misrepresented".

The carrier left California in November for the South China Sea and was sent to the Middle East ahead of attacks on Iran in February.

The deployment, which was originally set to end in May, has been repeatedly extended. No return date has been announced, but on Thursday multiple outlets reported the US is preparing to replace the carrier with the USS George Washington as part of a previously scheduled rotation plan.

The BBC has contacted the Pentagon about those reports.

Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal listed the reported hardships on the carrier, where about 5,000 people are on board, in a letter to Hegseth: "Shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system, which have caused many care packages in route to the ship to be lost in transit for months."

"These reports warrant immediate attention," the Democrat, who serves on the Armed Services Committee, wrote, "but they also raise a broader question: whether the Navy can sustain the operational tempo now being demanded of its carrier force."

Fellow Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego called for the military to allow a congressional delegation to visit the ship and "conduct oversight investigation into this horrible situation," he posted on X, adding: "There is no reason to be denied access."

Citing two unnamed officials, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, reported that earlier this month a sailor went overboard and was recovered by a helicopter, treated by the medical department, and transferred off the ship for further care.

The circumstances of the incident are currently under investigation.

The Military Times and Stars and Stripes reported earlier this week that multiple service members had considered suicide by jumping overboard, according to their families. They said that being at sea for an extended period of time and the conditions on board were hurting some members' mental health.

Those conditions also reportedly included not being able to clean laundry for more than a week and not eating fresh food due to infrequent visits to ports, when troops are not always allowed to leave the ship.

California Congressman Mike Levin, a Democrat, summarised the issues on X as: "moldy showers, broken toilets, laundry down for weeks, long stretches with no hot water, a meal that came down to half a cup of rice and two tortillas. No soap, deodorant, or toothpaste."

Following those reports, a Navy official told the BBC they had not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship and that "traditional supply hubs" had been "disrupted by combat actions".

The Navy was currently putting a priority on delivering "mission-critical supplies" to the ship.

"First food, then hygiene items, then mail," the official said on Wednesday. "Current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional AC (air conditioning), and healthy meal options."

Hegseth, while speaking to reporters in Panama on Thursday, said the government makes sure "every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment".

"Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody," he said. "What they do in those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls - it's incredible."

Asked about the conditions on board, Olivia Wales, a spokeswoman for Trump, told reporters that both Hegseth and Trump were committed to ensuring the US military was "equipped with the resources necessary to counter any threat to the United States".

During other lengthy deployments, the Navy took steps to provide entertainment for troops, according to military publication Stars & Stripes, external, including bingo, art sessions, and a singing contest.

A study, external of 956 sailors released in January 2025 found that troops aboard US Navy ships suffer the highest rates of "serious psychological distress" in comparison to other branches of the US military.

The study cited "unique stressors, such as poor habitability, noise, and demanding schedules that leave inadequate time for sleep and rest".

Meanwhile, suicide remains a leading cause of death in the US Navy and Marines, according to an analysis of military data by USNI News, and veterans have higher rates of suicide than Americans who have not served in the military, according to the Veterans Administration.

World.title: Person fined after using foghorn to wake sleeping polar bear
World.content:
A person has been fined for using a foghorn to wake a sleeping polar bear in Norway's Svalbard archipelago, a local official said.

The incident happened earlier this month after someone sounded the alarm from onboard a vessel, which was sailing in a fjord in northwestern Svalbard - about 1,000 km (620 miles) from the North Pole.

On Thursday, a person - who has not been named - was fined 50,000 kroner (Â£3,890) over the incident, the governor of the territory confirmed.

Under local regulations in the region, "it is forbidden to needlessly disturb, attract or pursue a polar bear", which was declared a protected species in Svalbard in 1972.

About 250 polar bears were counted in the archipelago during the last scientific estimate, carried out in 2015.

In a statement, governor Lars Fause said when the vessel sailed past the animal "its occupants are said to have spotted a polar bear sleeping on land".

"A person on board then used the ship's foghorn, waking the animal, which moved to another location."

The individual has agreed to pay the fine.

It is not the first time people have been fined for disrupting animals in the Svalbard region.

In 2024, a tourist was fined 11,500 kroner (Â£900) for getting too close to a walrus.

The Svalbard Environment Act stipulates that all traffic on the archipelago must take place in a way that does not lead to unnecessary disturbance of local wildlife - which include polar bears, seals, whales, reindeer and arctic foxes.

World.title: Eurovision Song Contest 2027 to be held in Burgas, Bulgaria
World.content:
"[Burgas] is a vibrant, welcoming city on the Black Sea with a strong musical and cultural identity, and it has the ambition, infrastructure and passion needed to welcome the Eurovision family," Green said.

"For the first Eurovision Song Contest ever to be held in Bulgaria, we want to create something that feels truly Bulgarian while also being unmistakably Eurovision â a celebration that brings people together through music."

Bulgaria's fourth largest city was selected for its "strong overall proposition, combining the venue and technical potential" - including hotel capacity, transport and international travel.

Reacting to the news, Dara said: "I'm so happy that Bulgaria will host Eurovision, so be ready because we're going to scream! And I know that all of my seaside people are great at parties."

It may come as a surprise to some Eurovision watchers that the contest will be held there and not in the capital, Sofia.

Speaking at a press conference after the most recent song contest in May, the director of BNT, Milena Miltenova, said: "I'm so proud of Dara's performance. What she did last night was amazing. And I'm so proud to say welcome to Sofia next year."

Dara - the winning contestant - said something similar: "I'm so happy that you're coming to Sofia next year. I'm happy that it [Eurovision] is going to be in my home."

However, the EBU said Burgas was selected following a "competitive" process involving four Bulgarian cities.

World.title: Mangione lawyers to meet federal prosecutors amid reports of plea deal
World.content:
Attorneys for Luigi Mangione, who is accused of killing United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York, are meeting federal prosecutors on Friday amid US media reports of a potential plea agreement.

Mangione faces two federal charges of stalking resulting in death, each carrying a maximum sentence of life in prison. It was not immediately clear which charges are under discussion.

"There's a conference scheduled for 11 am on Friday, and that's all we can say at this time," Jamie McDonald, the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), said this week.

Mangione also faces a separate state trial over Thompson's death. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges in both cases.

Discussion of a plea deal does not guarantee one will be reached, and such arrangements can fall apart before they are finalised.

Deals must also be approved by the court, and a separate hearing is typically scheduled for the defendant to enter a new plea.

Federal prosecutors brought the stalking charges against Mangione, alleging he travelled between states and carried out electronic surveillance with the intention of killing or harming Thompson. Prosecutors allege those actions resulted in Thompson's death.

A federal judge threw out two other charges in January, including that of murder through use of a firearm, which had carried the possibility of the death penalty.

Mangione's attorneys, the SDNY, and Manhattan District Attorney's office did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

His attorneys have previously argued he should not be tried in both state and federal court. At the moment, the judges presiding over both cases have allowed the trials to proceed.

But if Mangione pleads guilty in his federal case, it could open the door for his attorneys to argue the state case runs afoul of double jeopardy â a constitutional protection that prevents an individual from being prosecuted twice for the same crime.

New York's state constitution has its own prohibition on double jeopardy, which, if invoked here, could have a knock-on effect on Mangione's upcoming state trial.

"If a federal prosecution has been completed on a matter, the state cannot prosecute the matter on those same facts," said Mitchell Epner, a white-collar attorney.

There is still little clarity on what happens to the state case in that scenario.

Mark Chutkow, a white-collar defence attorney at the Dkyema law firm, said it is "kind of a live issue".

Chutkow the judge in the state trial would have to determine whether the charges overlap enough to trigger New York's double jeopardy statute, while Manhattan prosecutors may argue their case is distinct enough to proceed.

Mangione's state trial is scheduled to begin on 8 September, while the federal trial is listed for January 2027.

World.title: Family of Irish plane crash victim awarded $29m in damages
World.content:
The widow of an Irish United Nations employee, who died in 2019 following a Boeing 737 Max crash in Ethiopia, has been awarded $29m (Â£21.5m) in damages.

A jury in Chicago in the United States awarded the sum to Michael 'Mick' Ryan's family after his widow Naoise Connolly Ryan brought a civil suit against the aircraft manufacturer.

Her lawyers have said the verdict "represents an important measure of accountability and justice".

A Boeing spokesperson said the company is "deeply sorry to all who lost loved ones" and they "respect" the right for families to "pursue their claims".

Michael Ryan, a father of two living in Cork but originally from County Clare, was among the 157 people killed on board the Ethiopian Airlines plane.

He had worked as an engineer with the United Nations World Food Programme.

World.title: Presidency extends policing bill submission deadline by eight days
World.content:
The Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill has extended by eight days the deadline for members of the public to submit memoranda and position papers on the proposed legislation.

The deadline, originally set for Thursday, 13 August, has now been moved to 5:00 p.m. on Friday, 21 August, Femi Gbajabiamila, the chairperson of the working group, said in a statement on Thursday.

Mr Gbajabiamila, who is also the chief of staff to President Bola Tinubu, explained that the extension is to give individuals, institutions and organisations additional time to prepare and submit their contributions to the proposed legislation.

In June, the National Assembly passed legislation to establish state policing, a key reform that President Tinubu says will help curb spiralling insecurity in Nigeria.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the federal government announced a seven-week roadmap, including a call for memoranda on how to seamlessly transition Nigeria from a unitary policing system to one that allows for state police.

The proposed legislation provides for state police services to be coordinated alongside the federal police under an expanded National Police Council, while introducing safeguards such as legislative confirmation of state police commissioners and independent state police service commissions to oversee recruitment and discipline

Despite hopes by proponents of state police, critics including former police chiefs say state governors are likely to abuse the system. However, this newspaper understands that the main objective of calling for public input is to address these concerns.

According to the working group, the extension will help ensure that the public can make well-considered contributions to the process of developing a new national policing framework.

The proposed legislation is expected to provide the operational, administrative, institutional and funding framework for an effective policing architecture capable of responding to Nigeria’s evolving security needs.

It is also expected to provide safeguards for accountability, professionalism and the protection of citizens’ rights.

The working group said the significance of the proposed reforms made broader public participation necessary, encouraging legal practitioners, civil society organisations, security sector professionals, state governments, professional bodies, academics, experts and interested members of the public to use the additional time to submit their views.

It identified sustainable funding, command and control structures, recruitment and training standards, operational jurisdiction, inter-agency coordination, accountability mechanisms and safeguards against political interference or abuse as among the critical issues requiring consideration.

READ ALSO: Tinubu to receive draft state police bill on 3 September Gbajabiamila says

“These considerations underscore the importance of robust stakeholder engagement in developing a framework that is effective, accountable, sustainable and responsive to the peculiar security needs of communities across the Federation,” the statement said.

All submissions must be made exclusively through the official National Policing Bill portal, before the new deadline.

The working group said it would present a final, implementation-ready draft of the National Policing Bill for onward legislative processing at the conclusion of its assignment.

World.title: Nigerian university suspends lecturer for claiming tricyclists earn more than professors
World.content:
The management of Abia State University (ABSU) has suspended a lecturer, Prof Nnamdi Nwaeze, from the Department of Economics in the Faculty of Economics and Management Sciences.

The ABSU spokesman, Chijioke Nwogu, announced the lecturer’s suspension in a statement on Thursday.

PREMIUM TIMES reliably gathered that Nwaeze, a professor, was suspended on Wednesday for his Facebook post in which he claimed that professors at ABSU earn less than N400,000 per month.

The professor’s post addressed the recently declared industrial action by the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU) at ABSU.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He claimed that he was familiar with issues that resulted in the industrial action, but chose not to raise them to avoid being tagged as an “enemy of the state” or dismissed for a “political statement.”

Nwaeze said that lecturers at ABSU were receiving the poorest remuneration and were the least paid among Nigerian universities.

He further claimed that lecturers at the university were still being paid under the 2009 ASUU/FG salary structure, rather than the 2024 structure, the recent December 2025 structure, which was not implemented at ABSU.

The lecturer then claimed that professors at ABSU earn less than ₦400,000 per month, while commercial tricyclists earn over ₦450,000 per month.

“Are you aware that professors in all the federal and most state universities now earn between N1.3m to N1.4m as against what is obtainable in ABSU?” he asked.

“In this same Abia State, a local government councillor who may not have an ordinary WAEC level certificate allegedly earns about N600,000 monthly.

“A House of Assembly member earns about ₦8 million net salary in Abia State. Most appointees of this government can pay the salary of a professor and still have enough to take care of their families and personal needs.”

Suspension

In the Thursday statement, Nwogu, who doubles as the deputy registrar of the university, said the social media post “is inimical to the interests of the university and uncomplimentary to the visitors of the university.”

Governor Alex Otti of Abia State is the visitor to the university.

The ABSU spokesman said the university management has constituted an investigative panel to probe the matter.

“The suspension takes immediate effect pending the outcome of the investigation by the panel,” he said.

World.title: Court rejects police remand application, grants bail to 5 suspects
World.content:
A Benin High Court on Wednesday rejected an application by the police seeking to remand five persons arraigned on a three-count charge of willful damage.

The suspects are Osaigbovo Idemudia, Osasere Eria, Michael Atohengbe, Osamu Sadis, and Osahon Ezekiel.

The suspects were charged with conspiracy and willful damage of property at the Owan Forest Reserve in Irue Village, Orhionmwon Local Government Area of Edo.

The police arraigned the suspects in connection with an alleged incident that occurred on 7 November 2025 at the forest reserve.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, the Vacation Judge, Terry Momodu, declined the application for remand and granted the defendants bail of ₦500,000 each, with one surety each.

In his ruling, Justice Momodu held that the alleged offences were of a simple nature.

He said that there was nothing before the court to establish that the defendants had breached or jumped the administrative bail earlier granted to them by the police.

He therefore ordered the five accused persons to remain available and to report weekly to sign the attendance register as part of the conditions attached to their bail.

World.title: Bayelsa, among Nigeria’s most polluted states, says environmentalist
World.content:
Nnimmo Bassey, director of the Health of Mother Earth Foundation (HOMEF), says Bayelsa is one of Nigeria’s most polluted states, given the hydrocarbon extraction associated with the oil and gas industry.

Mr Bassey, a renowned environmentalist, stated this during a one-day capacity-sharing programme with the people of Nembe on Thursday in the Nembe Local Government Area of Bayelsa.

According to him, Bayelsa is one of the most polluted states in Nigeria and possibly in the world.

He said the Bayelsa State Oil and Environment Commission Report, published in May 2023, recorded a per capita oil pollution level of 1.5 barrels of crude oil per person.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Bassey also cited the environmental assessment of Ogoniland conducted by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) as evidence of the devastating impact of oil pollution in the Niger Delta.

He said oil companies failed to adequately clean up polluted areas, alleging that some resorted to superficial measures rather than proper remediation.

“The environmental assessment of Ogoniland was commissioned by the Federal Government of Nigeria in 2006 and carried out by UNEP to determine the scale, impact and long-term consequences of oil pollution in Ogoniland, Rivers.

“The assessment, conducted between 2009 and 2011, represents one of the most comprehensive environmental studies ever undertaken in an oil-producing region,” he said.

Mr Bassey said the investigation involved extensive scientific fieldwork across the four Ogoni local government areas of Khana, Gokana, Tai and Eleme, as well as laboratory analysis and consultations with communities.

He urged oil companies to stop what he described as the systematic destruction of the Niger Delta, saying the region had been treated as a “sacrificial zone” since the early 1950s.

Mr Bassey lamented the adverse effects of oil and gas extraction, including massive deforestation and various forms of erosion affecting land and coastlines.

He noted that although the term “environmental genocide” used in describing the situation was weighty, the issue should not be treated with levity.

‘Pregnant women in Nembe are suffering from anaemia’

Also speaking, the Head of Administration, Nembe Local Government Area, Godson Jim-Dorgu, said the area had been adversely affected over the years by oil spillage from oil companies.

He said oil pollution had severely affected fish and farm produce, thereby worsening hardship among residents of Nembe, which he described as one of the areas most affected by oil spills.

Mr Jim-Dorgu called on the federal government and oil companies to commence the remediation of areas damaged by oil exploration and production activities.

He said that since the Santa Barbara oil spill, which lasted about six months, there had been no adequate cleanup of the affected area, adding that the situation had negatively affected aquatic life.

Also, the Director of Primary Health Care, Nembe LGA, Jude Pulemote, said oil exploration activities had contributed to health challenges among rural residents.

He said many pregnant women in Nembe are suffering from anaemia, adding that the disruption of livelihoods by oil activities had adversely affected host communities.

Mr Pulemote urged the federal and Bayelsa governments to ensure that appropriate measures were taken to address the challenges confronting Nembe.

He described it as one of the communities severely affected by oil exploration and exploitation in the Niger Delta.

World.title: WHO recommends Phase III trial of Ebola vaccine against Bundibugyo virus
World.content:
The World Health Organisation (WHO) has recommended a Phase III trial of an Ebola vaccine to test whether it can protect against Bundibugyo virus disease.

WHO Director-General, Tedros Ghebreyesus, disclosed this in a video posted on his official X account on Thursday.

Ghebreyesus said two vaccines specifically developed against the Bundibugyo virus had entered Phase I safety trials in humans. At the same time, new animal studies had shown promising evidence that Ervebo, an Ebola vaccine, could also provide cross-protection against the virus.

He said the findings prompted WHO to recommend Ervebo for inclusion in a Phase III trial, which the organisation hopes to begin as soon as possible.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, it is not yet known whether Ervebo can protect humans against Bundibugyo virus disease.

Mr Ghebreyesus said the Phase III trial would help establish whether the vaccine is safe and effective and could provide evidence needed to make it available for the current outbreak and future outbreaks.

No licensed vaccines

The development comes as the Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the DRC has become the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record.

As of Thursday, the country had recorded 4,449 confirmed cases and 2,061 deaths across five provinces and 53 health zones, according to the WHO.

The health agency said the outbreak was spreading faster than any previous Ebola outbreak at the same stage and could surpass the 2014–2016 West African outbreak, which remains the largest on record, with more than 28,000 cases and 11,000 deaths reported in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

Bundibugyo virus is one of the viruses in the Ebola family that can cause severe and often fatal disease in humans.

Unlike Ebola virus disease caused by the Ebola virus, there is currently no licensed vaccine specifically approved for the prevention of Bundibugyo virus disease.

WHO said in June that Ervebo, the only licensed and WHO-prequalified Ebola vaccine, is approved for Ebola virus disease but not for Bundibugyo virus disease.

The current outbreak was first detected in the DRC in May, following an unexplained cluster of deaths in Ituri Province that was investigated. Laboratory testing confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease, prompting the DRC government to declare its 17th Ebola outbreak.

Uganda also confirmed imported cases linked to the outbreak in the DRC. WHO subsequently determined that the outbreak in the two countries constituted a Public Health Emergency of International Concern.

Previous Bundibugyo virus outbreaks have had case fatality rates between 30 and 50 per cent, according to the WHO.

PREMIUM TIMES reported on 9 August that WHO had already recommended Ervebo for evaluation in a randomised clinical trial after reviewing evidence suggesting that it could provide some protection against Bundibugyo virus.

Treatment advancement

Mr Ghebreyesus also disclosed progress in research into treatments for Bundibugyo virus disease.

He said a WHO-sponsored partners trial had reached 100 patients.

The trial is assessing potential treatments for the disease and is intended to generate evidence on which therapies can improve outcomes for infected patients.

Mr Ghebreyesus said the milestone showed that research could be mobilised rapidly and responsibly even during a difficult outbreak.

He called on partners to support and accelerate the vaccine trial, while emphasising that the response requires collaboration among the DRC government, WHO, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and other partners.

World.title: WAEC defends 2026 WASSCE results amid social media criticism
World.content:
The West African Examinations Council (WAEC) has defended the credibility of the 2026 West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE) results following criticisms on social media.

The examination body, in a statement issued on Thursday, said it had observed a “recent wave of public commentary”, particularly from content creators and social media commentators, questioning the credibility of the results.

The statement was signed by Moyosola Adesina, Head of Public Affairs, WAEC Nigeria, on behalf of the Head of the National Office, Amos Dangut.

WAEC said it “welcomes constructive scrutiny” but urged members of the public to disregard unverified claims and use its official channels to raise concerns about their results.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Social media concerns

While the examination body did not specify the content of the claims it was responding to, there were widespread claims of glitches in the 2026 WASSCE results following their release on 5 August.

On X, a user, @winexviv, whose post generated more than 200,000 views, alleged a “disastrous glitch” in the newly released results, particularly affecting candidates who took the computer-based examination.

He wrote: “WAEC, you can’t toy with our children’s destinies. We will not allow it. The results need to be withdrawn immediately and fixed, or we will challenge you in court.”

The post attracted comments from other users who expressed similar concerns, and it was widely shared by blogs, leading to wider discussions about the credibility of the results.

WAEC, however, said the results were produced through the same marking, moderation and auditing procedures that have guided its examinations over the years.

The council said the 2026 WASSCE was conducted in accordance with its standard operating procedures and relevant educational policies, in cooperation with the Federal Ministry of Education.

WAEC defends marking process

In its latest statement, WAEC said every candidate’s script undergoes a multi-tiered system of marking, moderation and auditing.

The council said the process is guided by standardised marking schemes and supervised by vetted subject experts to ensure objective and fair scoring.

It also said it maintains procedures for candidates and other members of the public to submit queries or grievances through its offices nationwide and its verified online platforms.

“WAEC hereby reiterates its unwavering commitment to preserving the integrity of its assessment processes and safeguarding the interests of every candidate,” the council said.

2026 WASSCE results

WAEC released the results of the examination on 5 August, with its Head of National Office, Amos Dangut, announcing the outcome at a press briefing in Lagos.

According to the council, 1,200,514 candidates, representing 61.54 per cent of the 1,950,726 candidates who sat the examination, obtained credits in at least five subjects, including English Language and Mathematics.

A total of 1,687,378 candidates, representing 86.50 per cent, obtained credits and above in at least five subjects, irrespective of English Language and Mathematics.

Of those who obtained at least five credits, including English Language and Mathematics, 558,883 candidates, representing 28.65 per cent, were male, while 641,631, representing 32.89 per cent, were female.

The examination was conducted between 24 April and 19 June. WAEC said 1,959,668 candidates from 24,207 schools registered for the examination, while 1,950,726 eventually sat for it.

Results still being processed.

WAEC said the results of 1,834,695 candidates, representing 94.05 per cent of those who sat the examination, had been fully processed and released.

The results of 116,031 candidates, representing 5.95 per cent, were still being processed due to issues the council said were being resolved.

Mr Dangut said efforts were underway to complete the process and release the results of the affected candidates.

The council also withheld the results of 167,486 candidates, representing 8.59 per cent of the total candidates, over alleged examination malpractice.

The figure was lower than the 9.7 per cent recorded in the 2025 examination, according to WAEC.

Mr Dangut attributed many of the malpractice cases to the increasing use of mobile phones in examination halls and organised cheating in some schools.

He said the cases were being investigated and would be presented to the appropriate council committee for consideration and a final decision.

He added that affected candidates would be informed of the decisions through their schools and could seek redress through WAEC’s malpractice complaints platform.

World.title: The cloud revolution: Inside Nigeria’s bold drive for digital sovereignty, By Fom Gyem
World.content:
Ultimately, the National Sovereign Cloud Initiative marks the beginning of a new chapter in Nigeria’s digital evolution — one in which sovereignty extends beyond physical borders into cyberspace, where data is recognised as a strategic national asset and trusted digital infrastructure serves as a catalyst for innovation, economic growth and regional leadership.

In today’s interconnected world, every online bank transfer, e-commerce purchase, hospital record, government portal login and video conference relies on an unseen yet indispensable foundation: cloud infrastructure. While billions of people interact with digital services every day, few stop to consider the complex technological ecosystem that powers these experiences. Quietly operating behind the scenes, cloud infrastructure has become the backbone of the modern digital economy, supporting everything from smartphones and social media platforms to artificial intelligence (AI), financial technology (fintech) and critical national security systems.

As countries race to build resilient digital economies, cloud infrastructure is no longer viewed merely as a technological necessity; it has become a strategic national asset. At its core, cloud infrastructure comprises interconnected data centres, servers, storage systems, networking equipment, software and virtualisation technologies that deliver computing services over the internet. Rather than relying on individual computers or on-premises servers, organisations can securely access computing resources remotely, enabling greater flexibility, scalability and efficiency.

This transformation has fundamentally changed how governments and businesses operate. Organisations can now scale computing resources on demand, reduce infrastructure costs, improve operational efficiency and deploy digital services faster than ever before. Whether streaming a movie, attending an online class, booking a flight or processing millions of financial transactions, cloud infrastructure ensures that these services remain secure, reliable and accessible around the clock.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Beyond convenience, cloud infrastructure has become a cornerstone of economic competitiveness. Countries with robust cloud ecosystems attract technology investments, stimulate innovation, create high-skilled jobs and strengthen their digital economies. Cloud services facilitate digital trade, enable seamless cross-border business operations and provide the computing power required for emerging technologies such as AI, blockchain and the Internet of Things (IoT). They also enhance business continuity by distributing data across multiple locations, reducing the risks posed by hardware failures, cyberattacks and natural disasters, while ensuring that essential services remain operational.

Nigeria’s expanding digital economy has heightened the urgency of developing resilient cloud infrastructure. With millions of citizens relying on digital banking, e-commerce, online education, healthcare technologies and e-government services, the country requires secure, reliable and scalable digital systems capable of supporting future growth.

Recognising this imperative, policymakers have intensified efforts to strengthen local cloud capacity, improve data governance, encourage investment in data centres and establish standards that inspire confidence among businesses and international investors. These initiatives are expected to stimulate indigenous innovation, create employment opportunities, enhance public service delivery and position Nigeria as one of Africa’s leading digital economies.

For decades, nations measured sovereignty through the strength of their borders, military capabilities and economic resilience. Today, however, a new frontier has emerged: digital sovereignty. In an era in which government services, financial transactions, artificial intelligence and national security increasingly depend on digital infrastructure, a country’s ability to control, secure and govern its own data has become a defining measure of national development.

It was against this backdrop that government officials, private sector leaders, development partners, academics and technology experts gathered to witness what many described as a watershed moment in Nigeria’s digital transformation journey.

At the centre of the event was the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), which formally commenced the implementation phase of the National Sovereign Cloud Initiative (NSCI). Through the unveiling of a comprehensive regulatory framework, the agency signalled Nigeria’s determination to reshape its digital landscape. More than the signing of regulatory documents, the event represented a bold declaration of intent to build a trusted digital ecosystem capable of supporting innovation, safeguarding national interests and attracting global investment.

The highlight of the ceremony was the signing of three foundational regulatory instruments by NITDA Director-General, Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi. These included the National Cloud Computing Guideline, the National Cloud Technical Guideline and the National Digital Infrastructure Assurance Framework (NDIAF). Alongside the unveiling of the National Cloud Investment Strategy, these instruments establish the policy, governance and technical architecture required to guide cloud adoption, strengthen digital infrastructure assurance and stimulate long-term investment in Nigeria’s rapidly expanding digital economy.

The milestone marked the culmination of years of consultation involving government institutions, indigenous cloud providers, international hyperscale cloud companies, data centre operators and development partners. It also builds upon the Federal Government’s Cloud First Policy, ensuring that Nigeria develops cloud infrastructure that aligns with global best practices while protecting national interests.

Beyond policy formulation, NITDA plans to establish the Sovereign Cloud Governance Committee to provide strategic oversight of the initiative. Before October, the agency also intends to operationalise a national digital regulatory platform that will streamline the registration, assessment, certification and compliance processes for cloud service providers and digital infrastructure operators.

The certification programme is expected to become one of the most significant confidence-building mechanisms within Nigeria’s digital ecosystem. By certifying cloud providers, data centre operators, managed service providers, AI infrastructure providers and sovereign compute operators, the framework seeks to assure government institutions, financial organisations and businesses that certified providers meet nationally approved standards for security, resilience and operational excellence.

Ultimately, the National Sovereign Cloud Initiative marks the beginning of a new chapter in Nigeria’s digital evolution — one in which sovereignty extends beyond physical borders into cyberspace, where data is recognised as a strategic national asset and trusted digital infrastructure serves as a catalyst for innovation, economic growth and regional leadership.

If effectively implemented through sustained collaboration among government, regulators, industry and development partners, the initiative could become one of the defining milestones in Nigeria’s journey towards a resilient, secure and globally competitive digital future. In an increasingly digital world, the nations that control and protect their digital infrastructure will be best positioned to shape the future. Nigeria has now taken a decisive step in that direction.

Fom Gyem, a co-author of Bulding a Safer Digital Economy in Nigeria writes from Wuye District Abuja.

World.title: In Ethiopia, five detained journalists pressured to apologise for terrorism
World.content:
The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Ethiopian authorities to immediately release five journalists who have been in detention for three years awaiting trial, instead of pressuring them to admit to, and apologise for, taking part in a deadly insurgency in exchange for their freedom.

Gobeze Sisay, Meskerem Abera, Genet Asmamaw, Dawit Begashaw, and Abay Zewdu have refused to write such apology letters, which they regard as “self-incriminating,” their lawyer, Solomon Gezahagn, told CPJ. The five were detained in 2023 on terrorism charges in connection with their reporting on unrest in the Amhara region.

Solomon said prison officials had threatened his clients and separated them from other prisoners to compel them to write their own versions of a draft document shared by the government, in addition to promising to stop working as journalists.

“After keeping these five journalists behind bars for years and delaying their trials, Ethiopian authorities are now trying to blackmail them into confessing to crimes that they have already denied in court,” said CPJ Africa Program Coordinator Muthoki Mumo. “Authorities must stop humiliating and manipulating Gobeze Sisay, Meskerem Abera, Genet Asmamaw, Dawit Begashaw, and Abay Zewdu, withdraw the charges against them, release them, and ensure that they are free to continue their journalism.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Media reports said more than 300 politicians, journalists, and others facing terrorism charges related to the conflict in the Amhara region had been asked to sign apology letters.

The insurgency began in 2023 in response to a government decision to integrate regional militia into the federal army, which triggered protests. The Amhara Regional Special Forces refused to surrender their weapons, and the Fano militia took up arms against federal forces.

About 30 detainees refused to sign, saying they would not declare themselves criminals while continuing to contest the charges in court, the news reports said.

Government officials asked the journalists to write letters in which they “take responsibility” for the crisis, lives lost, and property destroyed in the “extremist” struggle, promise not to participate in similar activities, and consent to unspecified government action against them if they breach that commitment, Solomon said.

In February, a federal court ruled that the joint case against Gobeze, Meskerem, Genet, and Dawit had sufficient evidence to proceed. Repeated adjournments have delayed their defence until November 19.

The court has yet to rule on whether prosecutors have presented sufficient evidence for a separate case against Abay to proceed. His next hearing is scheduled for October 16.

If convicted, the journalists could face life imprisonment or the death penalty.

The government told the journalists that the proposed release process was a pardon, but Solomon told CPJ that Ethiopian law provides for pardons only after a defendant has been convicted and received a final sentence. As the five journalists’ trials have not concluded, their cases would need to be resolved through the withdrawal of charges or an amnesty, he said.

CPJ’s email requests for comment to the Ministry of Justice and Government Communication Service office did not immediately receive any responses, while an email to the Federal Prison Commission could not be delivered.
