We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has unveiled its first frigate to enter service in decades at a ceremony in the Baltic Sea port of Gdynia, where the ship was constructed. The development marks a major milestone in a 15 billion zloty (€3.5 billion) programme to modernise the ageing Polish navy and strengthen NATO’s maritime defences. “Poland is becoming a maritime power in the Baltic Sea,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a ceremony to name the new ship, which he attended alongside opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki in a rare show of unity. Na terenie PGZ Stoczni Wojennej w Gdyni prezydent RP Karol Nawrocki, @PremierRP @donaldtusk oraz wiceministrowie @MON_GOV_PL @magdasobkowiak i @pawelbejda uczestniczą w uroczystości chrztu pierwszej jednostki programu „Miecznik”, fregaty wielozadaniowej – przyszłego ORP Wicher. pic.twitter.com/X2ftjoKTLZ — Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) August 12, 2026 The ORP Wicher, a medium-sized warship designed for escort, air defence and other fleet protection duties, is the first of three multi-role frigates based on Britain’s Arrowhead 140 design being built under Poland’s Miecznik programme, the largest modernisation project in the history of the Polish Navy. It is due to be launched on Thursday in a complex manoeuvre involving its transfer and controlled launch from a semi-submersible barge. Shipyard officials have described the operation as one of the most demanding engineering projects undertaken by Poland’s shipbuilding industry. The three frigates are intended to form the core of Poland’s surface fleet and will replace Poland’s two current Oliver Hazard Perry-class frigates, which were constructed in the 1970s and transferred from the US Navy in the years 2000 and 2002. Ahead of Wicher’s launch, leading Polish officials attended the naming ceremony in Gdynia, including Tusk and Nawrocki, who are normally bitter rivals but have sought to present a more united front when it comes to national defence. “There can be no arguments or disputes when it comes to our country’s security,” said Tusk, who declared that Poland was seeking to play a role in “determining not only its own future, but also the entire region and Europe”. Nawrocki, meanwhile, said that the modernisation of the Polish navy “sends a clear message that we will develop our armed forces in every theatre – on water, on land, and in the air”. Both leaders also hailed the fact that the new frigates are being built in Poland itself, helping bolster the Polish shipbuilding industry. Prezydent RP @NawrockiKn w #Gdynia: Życzę, abyście zawsze szczęśliwie wracali do portu, któremu na imię Polska. pic.twitter.com/hHia2sCZfn — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) August 12, 2026 The contract for the three frigates was signed in 2021 between Poland’s state Armament Agency (AU) and a consortium led by state-owned defence group PGZ, with British defence firm Babcock and other foreign partners also involved. The project was initially valued at about 8 billion zloty but had risen to around 15 billion zloty by the end of 2023 following amendments. Construction of the second frigate in Gdynia’s military shipyard began in May 2025, while work on the third began in April this year. The programme is scheduled to be completed by the end of 2031. Swedish defence giant Saab has signed a strategic collaboration agreement with Polish state defence group PGZ. The firms will cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology, including establishing an underwater technology centre in Poland https://t.co/dykKjMIAzX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 The ships are more than 140 metres long and are based on Britain’s Arrowhead 140 design, developed by Babcock and adapted to Polish military requirements. The frigates will be equipped with British CAMM and CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles, naval guns and anti-ship missiles capable of striking targets at ranges of more than 200 km. Their missions will include protecting shipping lanes and critical energy infrastructure and taking part in NATO naval groups. NATO has launched a new military operation in the Baltic Sea, an idea promoted by Poland last year in response to sabotage targeting undersea cables.@donaldtusk said at today's summit that "all signs point to Russia" being responsible for the damage https://t.co/cBPdL1fKkK — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 14, 2025 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on a major defence procurement spree. It now has the highest relative defence budget in NATO and is also the alliance’s largest arms importer. In recent years, Poland has also increasingly oriented itself towards the Baltic region, forming closer economic, energy and military ties with allies around the sea. Last year, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership on defence and economic ties. They subsequently held their first ever bilateral military exercises in the Baltic. As part of its naval modernisation programme, Poland has selected Sweden’s Saab as the supplier for three advanced A26 stealth submarines in a deal worth around €4.5 billion. Poland has signed a €4.5 billion deal to buy three A26 submarines from Sweden. World.title: Negative views of Poland’s justice system have grown under Tusk government, finds state pollster
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The proportion of Poles who negatively assess their country’s justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law and ensure that courts function more effectively and independently. New polling by state research agency CBOS found that, in June this year, 61% of Poles had a negative view of the functioning of the justice system, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017, when the former Law and Justice (PiS) government was in power. Only 26% now positively assess the system, down from 28% in 2022 and 36% in 2017. The last time positive views were lower was in 2005 (22%). The findings come two and a half years after the current government, a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, came to power in December 2023, replacing the national-conservative PiS administration. One of Tusk’s main promises was to restore the rule of law after eight years in which PiS had implemented a series of contested judicial reforms that experts, European courts and many Polish judges had condemned as undermining the independence and functioning of the judiciary. However, Tusk’s government has struggled to implement its promised changes. In many cases, its efforts have been blocked by PiS-aligned Presidents Andrzej Duda and Karol Nawrocki or other officials appointed under the former government. But in other cases, such as with a pledge to separate the functions of justice minister and prosecutor general, which were fused by PiS in 2016, the current ruling coalition has simply not followed through on its promises. In its latest polling, CBOS found that supporters of the current opposition are most dissatisfied with the functioning of the justice system: 72% of PiS voters have a negative view, as do 71% of those who support the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). However, even among voters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, a majority, 53%, have a negative opinion, with only 38% holding a positive one. Interestingly, public attitudes towards judges themselves have hardly changed. Currently, 19% of Poles have a positive view towards them and 23% a negative one. That is similar to findings in 2017 (22% positive, 24% negative) and 2012 (19% positive, 23% negative). More Poles (35%) think that the rule of law has got worse under Tusk's government than believe it has improved (24%). A further 28% think there has been no change, finds a new poll https://t.co/KkiuY2vDSW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2025 When asked to identify the greatest problems with the justice system, Poles instead often point to structural issues – that is, those that are under the control of politicians. The most commonly identified problem (chosen by 38% of respondents, who could select up to three main problems) was “prolonged proceedings” in court cases. The second biggest issue was “politicisation of courts” (18%). Only 4% said that “judges’ neglect of duty, incompetence and impunity” were among the biggest problems. However, 23% of respondents were unable to name a single major issue that the justice system faces. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 CBOS’s findings echo a number of other polls. After the first year of Tusk’s government, a survey by SW Research for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 35% of Poles thought the rule-of-law situation had got worse, compared to only 24% who thought it had improved. Another poll by the same agency for Onet, a news website, in January this year similarly found that 40% of Poles believe the justice system has not improved under the current government, while only 33% think it has got better. In response to the latter poll, justice minister Waldemar Żurek admitted to Onet that there had been problems in addressing the rule of law. But he blamed the “hurdles [put] in our path” by Presidents Duda and Nawrocki. Opposition-aligned President @NawrockiKn has vetoed a government bill intended to reform a judicial body at the heart of Poland’s rule-of-law crisis. He argued that the measures would simply create even greater “legal chaos” https://t.co/I7FHRKIoP1 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 19, 2026 In 2024, Duda refused to sign government bills overhauling the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which still contains judges illegitimately appointed under the former PiS administration. As a result, Tusk’s government refuses to recognise rulings issued by the TK. In February this year, Duda’s successor, Nawrocki, vetoed a government bill intended to restore the legitimacy of the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS), the body responsible for nominating judges to positions on courts. In 2017, the KRS was overhauled under PiS in a manner that rendered it illegitimate, according to multiple Polish and European court rulings. That in turn has led to doubts over the legal status of around 3,000 judges appointed by the KRS since 2017 and all the rulings issued by them. Nawrocki has also refused to swear in four new TK judges nominated by parliament this year, despite an order by the European Court of Human Rights that they be allowed to take up their positions. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Burgermeister to Open First Prague Restaurant on Wenceslas Square in 2027
World.content:
Berlin burger chain Burgermeister is preparing to enter the Czech market, with its first Prague restaurant expected to open in early 2027.

The company has chosen Wenceslas Square for its debut. The location will also serve as a base for Burgermeister’s planned expansion across the Czech Republic, with more restaurants already in the pipeline.

Burgermeister has built its reputation in Berlin over the past two decades, growing from a single restaurant in a former public toilet into an international chain with 32 locations across Germany and other European markets.



Burgermeister has not yet revealed the exact address or confirmed a specific opening date.

The Prague restaurant will follow the concept that made Burgermeister popular in Berlin. The chain focuses on freshly prepared burgers and fries, with part of its food production handled in-house. Its operations also include its own bakery.

From a former public toilet to an international burger chain

Burgermeister opened its first restaurant in the Kreuzberg district of Berlin in 2006. The location was far from a conventional restaurant site. It occupied a former public toilet beneath the railway tracks near Schlesisches Tor station.

The unusual setting quickly became part of the brand’s identity. Over the years, Burgermeister expanded beyond its original Berlin location and developed into a larger restaurant chain.

Today, the company has 32 branches and is pursuing its goal of building a pan-European network.

World.title: This Website Tracks How Many Trams Are Still Running Without Air Conditioning
World.content:
A new website is giving Prague residents a live picture of how many trams are operating without air conditioning, highlighting an issue that has become particularly noticeable during the city’s summer heat.

The service, Smrdime.cz, was created by developer Christoph Korb. Its name is a play on the Czech word smrdíme, meaning “we stink,” and refers to the uncomfortable conditions passengers can face inside overheated trams.

The website uses live data to calculate the share of Prague’s trams that are currently running without air conditioning. The figures change throughout the day as new vehicles enter and leave service.

When the service was checked on Thursday, August 13, Prague was experiencing temperatures of around 37 degrees Celsius. At that point, 188 of the 256 trams in operation did not have air conditioning, representing about 71 percent of the fleet being tracked.



Of the 147 air-conditioned trams available, 77 were operating at the same time.

The figures provide a snapshot rather than a fixed daily total. As trams are taken out of service and replaced, the balance between air-conditioned and non-air-conditioned vehicles changes continuously.

The project draws attention to a long-standing issue facing Prague’s public transport system: a substantial part of the city’s tram fleet still lacks air conditioning.

The website is based on data from two publicly available sources. Transport information comes from Golemio, Prague’s open-data platform, while weather information is provided by Open-Meteo. The two data sources are used to calculate the current situation displayed on the site.

Korb built the service with Anthropic’s Claude Code development tool. He has also published the project’s source code on GitHub, allowing other developers to inspect the project and contribute to its development.

World.title: From a Student’s Dream to a Japanese Bakery in Prague: The Story Behind Yaki-Pan
World.content:
For Hoan, opening a bakery in Prague was not a sudden business idea. It was a dream that had been taking shape for more than a decade.

After arriving in Prague as a student, Hoan watched members of the Vietnamese community build businesses across the city, most commonly in restaurants, grocery shops and nail salons.

She worked in grocery stores and restaurants herself, gradually gaining experience in the food industry while studying.

But after finishing school, she still was not sure what kind of business she wanted to open.



One thing was clear: she loved baking.

“Its my dream. It’s been my plan for a long time, more than 10 years,” she says.

Rather than opening another coffee shop, she decided to focus on what she knew best. She had visited bakeries around Prague and noticed what she saw as a gap in the city’s food scene: there were few places specialising in Japanese-style baking.

Around six years ago, she decided that she wanted to fill that gap herself.

The result was Yaki-Pan, a small bakery built around Japanese pastries and flavours. Before opening, Hoan spent roughly a year and a half — and much of that time at home — testing recipes and trying to recreate the textures and flavours she associated with Japanese baking.

Getting there was not straightforward.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Yaki-Pan (@yakipan_brunch)

Learning to work with Czech ingredients

For Hoan, authenticity was essential. She wanted the pastries at Yaki-Pan to resemble Japanese baked goods as closely as possible, but she quickly discovered that one of the most important ingredients presented a major challenge: flour.

Japanese flour differs significantly from the flour commonly available in the Czech Republic. The differences affect the texture, consistency and ultimately the finished pastry.

“The flour here is not the same as when I learnt,” she says.

Instead of simply following recipes she had learned elsewhere, Hoan had to adapt them to local ingredients. She experimented with different combinations of flour and spent months trying to achieve the texture she was looking for.

Three years ago, she travelled to China to study Japanese baking under professionals. There, she was able to work with Japanese ingredients and gain further experience. Returning to Europe meant starting another process of adjustment.

She considered importing Japanese flour to the Czech Republic, but eventually found it difficult to maintain as a long-term solution. Instead, she continued experimenting with locally available ingredients.

“I needed to test for about two years at my home,” she says.

The process has not necessarily ended with the bakery’s opening. Hoan continues to work on her recipes and ingredients, looking for ways to improve the pastries while staying as close as possible to the style she wants to create.

A warm welcome from Prague

If Hoan was worried that Japanese flavours might be unfamiliar to Prague customers, the first day quickly put those concerns to rest.

When Yaki-Pan opened, she had not prepared significantly more food than usual. Within 30 minutes, the bakery had sold out.

The first two months were particularly busy, especially at weekends. Today, the customer base includes tourists, Japanese residents and visitors who have become regulars.

Japanese customers have also played an important role in validating Hoan’s approach, frequently complimenting her on how closely the pastries resemble those they know from Japan.

Among the most popular items is shio-pan, a Japanese-style bread known for its soft texture and salty flavour. At Yaki-Pan, the vegan version has become one of the bakery’s bestsellers and regularly sells out.

Hoan’s own favourite pastry, meanwhile, changes from day to day.

The bakery’s success has also brought an unexpected question. Some customers have asked why a Vietnamese woman decided to open a Japanese bakery.

For Hoan, the answer is simple. “It’s my dream,” she says. “I put all my energy into my recipes.”

Her background, she suggests, is less important than the work she has put into learning the craft and developing the food.

Building Yaki-Pan’s future

For now, Hoan is focused on the bakery she has already built. Yaki-Pan is run by Hoan and her husband, and her previous experience working in restaurants has helped her manage the busy days herself.

The couple are already thinking about the next stage. They hope to add outdoor seating next year and, eventually, open another location.

But there is no immediate rush to expand.

“Now I want to put all my energy into this one,” Hoan says.

There are also plans to introduce another type of matcha, giving customers more choice alongside the bakery’s existing drinks.

For a business that began as an idea Hoan carried with her for more than 10 years, Yaki-Pan remains very much a work in progress. The recipes continue to evolve, customers continue to discover Japanese-style baking, and Hoan is still searching for the ingredients and techniques that bring her original vision closest to reality.

World.title: Prague Taxi Driver Arrested After Taking CZK 3.5 Million Left in His Car
World.content:
A 21-year-old taxi driver in Prague has been arrested after allegedly taking a suitcase containing CZK 3.5 million in cash that passengers accidentally left in his car.

The money was recovered by police after the driver eventually admitted what he had done and told investigators where he had hidden it. He now faces up to five years in prison.

The incident happened in late July, although police only released details of the case several days later.



The passengers were a married couple who had taken a taxi to Václav Havel Airport in the early morning. They were heading on vacation and only realized after reaching the airport that one of their suitcases was still in the vehicle.

The couple immediately contacted the driver and asked him to bring the suitcase back. According to police, he initially agreed, but the luggage never appeared despite further calls and reminders.

The couple eventually reported the matter to police. Given the amount of money involved, forensic specialists from the Prague 1 police precinct joined the investigation.

Investigators quickly located the taxi and detained the driver. A search of the vehicle, however, produced no suitcase.

The 21-year-old initially denied that the passengers had left anything behind, telling police that he had not found any luggage in the car.

His account later changed.

After being placed in a cell, the man confessed and revealed where he had hidden the cash. Police officers and forensic specialists then located the money in a forest near Kladno.

The investigation also uncovered an attempt to destroy evidence. Near the cash, investigators found the burned remains of the suitcase. Police say the driver had taken the items to the forest, piled them together and set them on fire.

The driver remains under investigation and could face a prison sentence of up to five years if convicted.

World.title: Six Prague Rooftops and Terraces to Visit Before Summer Ends
World.content:
Summer is already moving on, and Prague’s rooftop season won’t last much longer.

August is the time to make the most of the city’s terraces, sunset views and outdoor events before they disappear for another year.

Here are six rooftops and terraces worth visiting before autumn arrives.



1. REASON at Masaryčka

Eleven floors above Masaryk Station, REASON offers one of Prague’s newest rooftop dining spots, with views over the city and the Zaha Hadid-designed Masaryčka development.

This summer, its terrace is also home to the seasonal Frerejean Frères Champagne Bar, serving champagne by the glass, cocktails, oysters and light bites. The menu includes THE REASON KIR, made with herbs grown on the rooftop.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and cocktails above Masaryčka.

2. W Prague – ABOVE Rooftop

ABOVE Rooftop at W Prague brings a Mediterranean feel to the top of Wenceslas Square.

The daily Mediterranean Hour runs from 5 to 6 PM, with two spritzes and a Taste of the Mediterranean platter for CZK 990. Oysters are also served from Thursday to Saturday, alongside a programme of summer events and pop-ups.

This summer: Mediterranean Hour, sunset drinks and oysters in the centre.

3. MINUTY Rooftop Terrace

The rooftop at Fairmont Golden Prague offers views across Pařížská, Letná and the city centre from nine floors up.

MINUTY Rooftop Terrace by Golden Eye focuses on champagne, oysters, caviar and cocktails. The terrace is seasonal and is expected to remain open until September, weather permitting.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and caviar with a view.

4. Sky Lounge 360°

For the view alone, Sky Lounge 360° is hard to beat. The rooftop looks across Prague’s historic centre and becomes livelier during the summer months, with DJs, sunset events and Prague Rooftop Festival activities.

It is more about drinks and atmosphere than a long dinner — a good option for an evening that starts at sunset and continues after dark.

This summer: Sunset events, DJs and panoramic views.

5. Casablanca Sky Bar

On the sixth floor of The President Hotel, Casablanca Sky Bar looks out over the Vltava and Prague skyline.

With DJs, cocktails and regular sunset events, it has more of a party atmosphere than a traditional hotel rooftop. It is also one of the venues taking part in the Prague Rooftop Festival.

This summer: DJs, cocktails and sunset parties above the Vltava.

6. Monkey Bar

Monkey Bar at Falkensteiner Hotel Prague is a quieter alternative, with a green, jungle-style terrace close to the main railway station.

Every Thursday until the end of August, the terrace hosts BBQ & Beats, combining barbecue, live music and summer drinks. Frozen margaritas are also on the menu.

For daytime plans, there is Jungle Brunch, including a bottomless mimosa option.

This summer: BBQ & Beats every Thursday through August.

World.title: Czech Rivers Reach Record Lows as Drought Deepens
World.content:
Rivers and streams across the Czech Republic are experiencing exceptionally low flows as a prolonged drought continues to worsen, with several waterways approaching or reaching their lowest levels since records began.

According to the latest data from the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute, the vast majority of monitored rivers and streams are flowing well below their long-term averages.

Some of the country’s smallest watercourses have dried up completely, while critical conditions are emerging on several major rivers.



The Elbe is among the most affected. Its flow has fallen to one of the lowest levels ever recorded and is approaching the historic minimum for the entire period of regular observations.

The Vltava is in a somewhat better position in some sections because the reservoir system is being regulated to help stabilize water levels. But even the Vltava has reached an unprecedented low in České Budějovice, where the river is recording its lowest measured flow.

The effects of the drought are particularly visible at the Orlík Reservoir. As water levels have fallen sharply, the remains of a former hydroelectric power plant at Dubrava have emerged from beneath the reservoir.

The plant was built in 1929 but was demolished and flooded in the 1960s when the Orlík Reservoir was created. Its remains have now resurfaced as the reservoir continues to shrink.

The worsening conditions are not limited to rivers and reservoirs. Groundwater levels are also declining, affecting wells and raising concerns about the availability of water supplies in some areas.

Hydrologists are not expecting a significant improvement in the coming days. According to the medium-range weather forecast, there are currently no clear conditions that would bring a substantial recovery in river flows or groundwater levels.

World.title: How to Find a GP in Prague When Practices Aren’t Accepting New Patients
World.content:
Finding a general practitioner in Prague can look simple until the first calls begin.

One practice does not answer. Another says it is full. A third can offer an appointment, but not in English. Your insurer’s list may not show who is accepting new patients today or what kind of visit is available.

If registration is blocked, first clarify whether you need long-term GP care, a one-time consultation, a specialist, an urgent route, or a private self-paid visit.



Decide whether this is really a GP problem

A GP is often the right first contact for common health concerns, preventive care, prescription questions, basic tests, and referrals. In Czech, this doctor is called a praktický lékař.

Not every situation should wait for GP registration. For a sudden and serious health problem or a possible threat to life, call 155 for the medical emergency service or 112 for the European emergency number.

If the issue clearly belongs to a dentist, gynaecologist, or specialist, ask that provider whether direct booking is possible or a referral is required. Patients in Czechia can generally approach a specialist without a GP referral, but an individual provider, insurer, or procedure may have its own requirements.

Tell the provider if you already have results, imaging, a hospital discharge report, or a specialist recommendation, because those documents may affect the next step.

Ask your insurer for help finding a provider

If you have Czech public health insurance and cannot find a GP, contact your insurer directly. Czech health insurers are responsible for helping their members access contracted care under the applicable rules on geographical and time availability.

Ask for practical information:

• Which contracted GPs in my area should be available to new patients?

• Which providers can communicate in English?

• Does the provider have a contract for my care?

• Do I need a referral, approval, or particular documents?

Availability can change, so confirm the details with the practice before travelling there.

If you have commercial insurance, check the provider network and approval process in your policy or contact the insurer. Do not assume that a clinic visit is covered simply because the clinic appears in a search result.

Understand why a practice may say no

A practice may lawfully refuse to accept a patient into care for reasons such as capacity, operational limits, distance that prevents home visits, or the absence of a contract with the patient’s public insurer.

If a provider refuses to accept you as a patient, ask for written confirmation with the reason. This gives you something concrete to show your insurer when requesting another available provider.

Clarify whether the refusal covers long-term registration, all appointments, only publicly insured care, the requested language, or a service the practice does not provide. A limited “no” does not necessarily close every route.

Separate registration from a one-time appointment

Registration and a medical appointment are related, but they are not identical.

Registration creates a long-term relationship with a primary-care doctor. It matters for continuity and for services whose public-insurance reimbursement is linked to the registered GP.

A provider may also offer care without registering you, particularly through a one-time, self-pay appointment. The scope and payment conditions vary, so never assume that a single consultation also means registration or that public insurance will cover it.

Before booking, ask whether the offer is long-term registration, a one-time consultation, a preventive check-up, an urgent appointment, specialist care, or a self-paid visit. Do not leave a clinic assuming that one consultation means you are registered there.

Prepare the information the provider needs

Share only enough information for the provider to understand the request, and use its approved secure channel for medical documents.

Prepare:

• the main reason for the appointment;

• how long the issue has been present;

• whether the request is routine, worsening, urgent, or preventive;

• your insurer or intention to self-pay;

• your preferred language;

• current medicines and allergies;

• relevant reports, results, imaging, or referrals.

A concise request helps the provider determine whether it can help and which appointment type is appropriate.

Make sure the visit has a clear ending

Getting an appointment is only the first part of the process.

A doctor may order tests, issue a referral, prescribe medication, or recommend another consultation. It should be clear who will explain the results and arrange the next step.

Before leaving, ask:

• What happens next?

• When should I expect the results?

• Who will explain them?

• Do I need another appointment?

• Should I send anything to another doctor?

A useful appointment should leave you knowing what comes afterwards.

When coordination support can help

OpenMedical helps patients find suitable English-speaking GPs and other medical specialists in Prague, confirm current availability and appointment conditions, and coordinate the booking process. The service also helps prepare documents, communicate with selected providers, and keep follow-up steps clear.

Quick checklist when GP registration is blocked

• Decide whether the situation is an emergency or can wait for a planned appointment.

• Ask your public insurer to help identify an available contracted provider.

• Ask the practice whether its refusal applies to registration or to all appointments.

• Request written confirmation if a provider refuses to take you into care.

• Confirm language, payment route, referral requirements, and whether a one-time appointment is available.

• Keep copies of medical reports and results.

• Before leaving an appointment, confirm who will explain the results and arrange the next step.

Finding a GP in Prague can take patience. A blocked registration does not mean there is no possible way forward. It means the next route needs to be identified more precisely.

Questions to ask before confirming a GP appointment

• Are you accepting new registered patients?

• Is this a registration visit or a one-time consultation?

• Can the appointment be handled in English?

• Do you have a contract with my public health insurer?

• What is the price if the appointment is self-paid?

• Do I need a referral or prior approval?

• Which documents should I provide, and how should I send them securely?

• How will results and further steps be handled?

World.title: Medal rush for Hungary at the European Aquatics Championships as Milák, Kós and relay strike gold – VIDEO
World.content:
Hungary enjoyed a spectacular evening at the European Aquatics Championships in Paris on Thursday, with Kristóf Milák setting a European record in the men’s 100m butterfly before helping the Hungarian men’s 4x100m freestyle relay claim a historic gold medal with a national record.

The two victories capped an outstanding day for Hungarian swimming, while Olympic champion Hubert Kós also produced another strong performance, finishing fourth in the 100m butterfly with a personal best.

According to MTI, Milák won the butterfly final in 49.48 seconds, breaking the European record and finishing just 0.03 seconds outside Caeleb Dressel’s world record.

Milák delivers European record at the European Aquatics Championships

The defending European champion and Olympic champion had to fight for the victory until the closing metres.

The field remained tightly packed after the turn, with at least four swimmers still in contention for gold. Milák, however, produced a superb final ten metres, moving clear of his rivals to clock the second-fastest performance in history.

France’s Maxime Grousset took silver in 49.70 seconds, while Switzerland’s Noè Ponti finished third in 49.93.

Kós narrowly missed the podium after swimming a personal best of 50.25 seconds, good enough for fourth place.

The Hungarian pair had already demonstrated their strength during Wednesday’s programme. Kós had won the 200m backstroke with what MTI described as the fifth-fastest performance of all time, while Milák finished third in the 100m freestyle with one of the fastest times ever recorded in the event.

Despite those demanding races, both arrived at Thursday’s butterfly final in strong form.

European Aquatics Championships – Kristóf Milák with his gold medal. Photo: MTI

Men’s 100m butterfly results

Kristóf Milák (Hungary) – 49.48, European record Maxime Grousset (France) – 49.70 Noè Ponti (Switzerland) – 49.93 Hubert Kós (Hungary) – 50.25, personal best

Interesting analysis – The shocking truth about Hungarian football finances: clubs are funded not by the fans, but from the central budget

Historic relay gold for Hungary

The medal rush continued later in the evening as Hungary won the men’s 4x100m freestyle relay for the first time in European Championships history.

The final line-up of Hubert Kós, Szebasztián Szabó, Nándor Németh and Kristóf Milák touched the wall in 3:10.03, setting a new Hungarian record and European Championships record.

Russia, competing under neutral status, finished second in 3:10.12, while Croatia claimed bronze in 3:11.08.

Hungary had qualified for the final with the fifth-fastest time in the heats, but the team was significantly strengthened for the medal race by the arrival of Olympic champions Kós and Milák.

Kós opened the relay with a personal best of 48.18 seconds, cutting almost seven-tenths from his previous best.

Szabó briefly moved Hungary into the lead before handing over in fifth place, while Németh closed the gap and sent Milák into the final leg only 0.01 seconds behind the leader.

Milák produces stunning anchor leg

Milák then delivered one of the standout relay performances of the championships.

With the advantage of a flying relay start, he split 46.29 seconds over the final 100 metres and overtook the Russian team in the closing strokes to secure gold for Hungary.

The overall winning time of 3:10.03 improved the previous Hungarian national record of 3:11.06, set by the team that finished fifth at the Tokyo Olympics.

Men’s 4x100m freestyle relay results

Hungary – 3:10.03, national and European Championships record

Hubert Kós, Szebasztián Szabó, Nándor Németh, Kristóf Milák Neutral athletes – 3:10.12

Ivan Girev, Vasily Kukushkin, Aleksandr Shchegolev, Egor Kornev Croatia – 3:11.08

If you missed it: Hungarian swimmer ranked world’s second best, says prestigious outlet

Kós adds another Hungarian gold in the 200m backstroke

Hungary’s success at the European Aquatics Championships had already begun before Milák’s record-breaking performance, with Hubert Kós claiming gold in the men’s 200m backstroke in Saint-Denis.

Kós took control of the race immediately and was inside world-record pace at the 50-metre mark. By halfway, he was around eight-tenths of a second ahead of the pace set by former world-record holder Aaron Peirsol.

Although he could not maintain that speed over the second half of the race, the Hungarian remained comfortably in front and touched the wall in 1:53.08, securing Hungary’s first gold medal in pool swimming at this year’s European Championships.

Greece’s Apostolos Siskos finished second in 1:53.81, while Italy’s Thomas Ceccon took bronze in 1:53.96.

Kós’s winning time was also historically significant: 1:53.08 is tied for the fifth-fastest performance ever recorded in the event. The Hungarian already owns another of the fastest 200m backstroke performances in history, further strengthening his position among the discipline’s leading swimmers.

Pádár reaches the 200m freestyle final

There was further positive news for Hungary in the women’s 200m freestyle. Nikolett Pádár finished third in her semi-final in 1:57.24 and qualified for the final with the seventh-fastest time overall.

A golden evening for Hungarian swimming

The two victories gave Hungary two gold medals on Thursday evening alone at the European Aquatics Championships, underlining the strength of a men’s team built around several Olympic champions and internationally established swimmers.

Milák was the central figure of the night, first coming within three hundredths of a second of the 100m butterfly world record and then producing the decisive final leg in the relay.

Kós also played a key role, adding a fourth-place finish and two personal bests to his earlier European title in the 200m backstroke.

For Hungary, Thursday’s performances represented not only another haul of medals in Paris, but also a series of national, continental and championship-level benchmarks that made it one of the strongest sessions of the tournament so far.

World.title: Government press conference: Paks nuclear power plant faces shutdown risk
World.content:
The Danube has begun falling again at Paks, increasing the threat of further restrictions or even a complete shutdown at the Paks nuclear power plant, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said on Thursday. The government has already begun emergency river-engineering works, while two 80-metre barges are being prepared for possible deployment if the water level drops faster than expected.

According to MTI, the water gauge at Paks stood at around minus 119-120 centimetres on Thursday afternoon. Magyar said even a few centimetres can now make a significant difference to the operation of Hungary’s only nuclear power station.

For foreign readers, the negative figures refer to the local water gauge datum and do not mean that the river itself has a negative depth.

Paks nuclear power plant approaching critical water levels

Experts expect the gauge to fall to around minus 121 centimetres on Friday morning and potentially reach minus 132 centimetres by Sunday or Monday, Magyar said.

That is a crucial threshold. If the river falls to minus 132 centimetres, one of the two turbines currently operating would again have to be shut down.

The medium-term outlook is even more concerning. According to the prime minister, the level could reach minus 136-137 centimetres within six or seven days. At minus 140 centimetres, the entire Paks nuclear power plant would have to be taken offline.

At present, only two of the plant’s eight turbines are operating, producing almost 500 megawatts of electricity.

Magyar stressed that Danube levels can be forecast with reasonable confidence only a few days in advance, rejecting claims that the exact severity of the current situation could have been predicted months ago.

The crisis is not unique to Hungary. Romania began shutting down the last operating reactor at its Cernavodă nuclear power plant on Thursday because of historically low Danube levels, after its other reactor had already been taken offline in late July.

Emergency bed sill already under construction

The government’s main intervention is the construction of a riverbed sill between Paks and Dunaszentbenedek, close to the nuclear plant’s cold-water intake channel.

The structure is intended to raise the upstream water level sufficiently to maintain the cooling-water supply required by the plant.

Around 145,000 cubic metres of rock are planned to be placed in the Danube. The first 35,000 cubic metres will form a transverse rock ridge designed to produce a meaningful rise in the water level. Another 110,000 cubic metres will later reinforce the riverbed and protect the structure against erosion caused by the Danube’s current.

The project is technically challenging. Gacsályi József, deputy technical director-general of Hungary’s National Directorate General for Water Management, said around 800 cubic metres of water per second currently pass through the river section where the structure is being built.

The sill will be constructed across a section of roughly 300 metres between the plant’s cold- and warm-water channels.

Work is taking place on both banks. Hungarian soldiers are working primarily on the left bank, which can be accessed on dry ground, while contractors and water-management specialists are operating on the deeper right-hand side.

Heavy machinery is already arriving, access roads and storage areas are being prepared, and the first quantities of rock have been delivered.

The government wants the crucial part of the structure completed within about 30 days, with construction continuing around the clock.

As we wrote today – The danger is not over: Budapest water supply under pressure again

Two barges could provide rapid emergency relief

A second, faster intervention is also being prepared.

Two approximately 80-metre barges are to be positioned downstream of the cold-water intake and secured to piles on the right bank. They would be placed at an approximately 45-degree angle rather than perpendicular to the shore.

The vessels are intended to act as temporary flow-control structures. According to modelling presented at the briefing, partially sinking the barges could immediately raise the water level by around 10-15 centimetres, while the full deployment of one barge could potentially produce an increase of about 20 centimetres.

The two barges would create a combined diversion structure roughly 160 metres long.

They are expected to be ready for testing from Friday so that they can be used rapidly if the Danube falls below the critical level earlier than forecast.

However, the government regards their use as a last-resort measure. Magyar warned that an uncontrolled barge could create serious problems if it broke free, became lodged in the river or obstructed the plant’s warm-water outlet.

As we wrote today, Danube water level falling again. Major intervention planned to protect Paks nuclear plant – pictures

Construction to continue into the autumn

Preparatory work on the left bank is scheduled to accelerate between 15 and 18 August, including clearing the route and installing geotextile material.

A pontoon structure on the right bank is planned between 17 and 21 August to allow rock to be delivered directly into the riverbed.

Rock placement will then proceed from both sides during late August and early September, with the two sections of the water-raising ridge expected to be joined by around 11 September. Additional reinforcement work is planned to continue into October.

The project is designed ultimately to guarantee a gauge level of around minus 90 centimetres at Paks, which the government says would allow the nuclear plant to operate at full capacity.

Emergency project to cost EUR 16.9 million

The government currently estimates the gross cost of the Paks-Dunaszentbenedek bed sill at HUF 6.165 billion, or approximately EUR 16.9 million at the official 13 August exchange rate.

The figure includes the reconstruction of affected road sections and rehabilitation of the riverbanks.

Funding will come from Hungary’s national emergency reserve, while the budget of the National Directorate General for Water Management will be opened to cover the project.

Magyar said spending would be closely monitored and contractors would be required to account for all expenditure.

The government has also received private-sector offers of assistance. Austria’s Strabag has offered technology, transport and materials free of charge, according to the prime minister, while Hungarian-owned KÉSZ Group has also made an offer.

Magyar criticised major companies associated with the former Fidesz government for what he described as a lack of similar offers.

Full shutdown could cost HUF 50 billion a month

The financial stakes are significantly larger than the cost of the emergency intervention.

According to Magyar, a complete loss of production at Paks would cost the state budget at least HUF 50 billion, or roughly EUR 137 million, every month. That estimate does not include the additional cost to businesses and the wider economy of replacing domestic nuclear generation with more expensive electricity imports.

The prime minister estimated that the water shortage and reduced Paks production are currently cutting around 0.1% from Hungary’s GDP, although he stressed that precise calculations are not yet available.

Maintaining Paks output is particularly important because the nuclear station normally plays a central role in Hungary’s electricity supply. Recent record-low Danube levels have already forced the plant to operate far below its usual capacity.

Nuclear safety limits the available solutions

Government officials said numerous engineering options had been considered with water-management, energy and nuclear experts.

Some were rejected because nuclear safety had to remain the overriding consideration, Magyar said. The government ultimately selected the riverbed sill and possible deployment of barges as what it considers the safest, most effective and most cost-efficient immediate combination.

The National Atomic Energy Office has been monitoring the project since the planning stage, while engineers from the Budapest University of Technology and Economics contributed to the modelling.

The Defence Administration Office is coordinating the numerous state bodies, contractors and military units involved.

Magyar described the situation as the reverse of a flood emergency: instead of protecting infrastructure from too much water, authorities are attempting to maintain sufficient water levels to protect critical infrastructure.

Environmental approvals running alongside emergency work

The accelerated construction has also raised questions about environmental permitting.

The government has classified the situation as an emergency, allowing physical works to begin before all procedures have been completed. Officials stressed, however, that this does not eliminate environmental studies or the requirement to obtain permits.

Hydrobiologists and ecologists have been involved in planning, according to the water-management authority. The environmental authorisation process must begin by the end of September and will examine effects on wildlife and the river ecosystem.

A permanent operating permit for the sill will be possible only if the structure meets the relevant requirements.

Magyar said modelling suggests that the structure would increase Danube levels by no more than around one centimetre during a future flood, and therefore should not significantly increase flood risk.

Paks II and Hungary’s longer-term cooling strategy questioned

The emergency has also revived a broader debate over how Hungary’s nuclear power system should adapt to increasingly extreme river conditions.

Magyar said the government would examine the possibility of installing cooling towers or closed-loop cooling systems. Such investments would be expensive, but he said they could eventually become necessary for the lifetime extension of the existing Paks plant, the planned Paks II expansion, or both.

He also questioned whether the existing environmental and cooling permits for Paks II adequately reflect the river conditions Hungary is now experiencing.

The government is preparing broader climate and water-management strategies, including the “Water into the Landscape” programme, while Magyar said Hungary would seek to make water management a priority during negotiations over the next EU budget.

He also argued that international agreements governing use of the Danube need to be reconsidered because many were drawn up for very different river-flow conditions.

Austria and Slovakia have complied with existing agreements, Magyar said, but the underlying hydrological situation has changed substantially.

If you missed it today: Russian Rosatom breaks silence as it builds Hungary’s newest nuclear reactors

Political dispute over responsibility for the crisis

The prime minister also used Thursday’s briefing to criticise Viktor Orbán’s former government, which governed Hungary for 16 years before Magyar took office in May 2026. Magyar accused the previous administration of failing to prepare sufficient long-term solutions for low Danube levels and of neglecting possible investments such as changes to Paks’s pumping infrastructure.

These were political allegations by the current government rather than findings presented as part of the technical assessment.

Magyar also criticised proposals circulating online, including suggestions involving dredging, blasting or large-scale pumping systems, arguing that some could endanger nuclear safety.

He separately attacked Mi Hazánk leader László Toroczkai over criticism of the decision to shut down Paks turbines, saying nuclear safety could not be compromised for the sake of maintaining electricity generation.

Low Danube levels becoming a long-term energy challenge

The government maintains that the emergency measures will prevent the Paks nuclear power plant from losing all of its generation capacity, but officials acknowledge that there is currently no clear indication of when the Danube will return to substantially higher levels.

That makes the crisis larger than an immediate engineering problem.

The government is preparing a wider energy plan covering wind power, electricity storage and greater diversification of energy sources. Magyar said Hungary needs more capacity to retain and store energy and must ensure that electricity is available from as many domestic and external sources as possible.

For Paks, meanwhile, the coming days remain decisive. The barges are being prepared for immediate use, while construction of the more permanent riverbed sill proceeds around the clock.

If the Danube continues to fall towards the minus 140-centimetre threshold before the interventions take effect, Hungary could still face the first complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant in its more than four decades of operation.

World.title: The shocking truth about Hungarian football finances: clubs are funded not by the fans, but from the central budget
World.content:
Hungarian football finances remain heavily dependent on centrally distributed funding rather than supporters buying tickets, according to a new analysis of the country’s top-flight league. NB I clubs generated more than HUF 63 billion (around EUR 173 million) in combined revenue in 2024, yet ticket and season-ticket sales contributed only about 4% of that total.

The figures were highlighted in an analysis published by Mfor, which examined how Hungary’s 12-team first division is financed and how the structure affects clubs’ business decisions.

For international readers, NB I – officially the OTP Bank Liga – is the highest tier of Hungarian club football and includes teams such as Ferencváros, Újpest and Paks.

Hungarian football finances rely far more on central money than fans

Corporate accounts analysed by G7 showed that NB I clubs collected roughly HUF 2.54 billion (EUR 7 million) from tickets and season tickets in 2024. Against total league revenue exceeding HUF 63 billion (EUR 173 million), matchday admission therefore generated only around 4% of revenue.

The difference becomes particularly striking when compared with the money distributed centrally for the current 2026/27 season.

The Hungarian Football Federation (MLSZ) announced in July that HUF 10.5 billion (EUR 28.9 million) will be distributed among the 12 NB I clubs during the season. The money is not divided equally, as payments depend partly on sporting and player-selection criteria.

By comparison, Mfor calculated that an entire season consisting of rounds with ticket income similar to the 2024/25 opening weekend would produce a theoretical gross ticket-value equivalent of about HUF 2.8 billion (EUR 7.7 million). The publication stressed that this is an estimate rather than clubs’ actual cash income.

Public broadcaster pays billions for television rights

Central financing is built from several major contracts.

According to the MLSZ, Hungary’s public broadcaster MTVA is paying HUF 6 billion (EUR 16.5 million) for broadcasting rights for the 2026/27 season. State-owned gambling company Szerencsejáték Zrt. is paying another HUF 6 billion (EUR 16.5 million) for marketing rights and HUF 3 billion (EUR 8.2 million) for betting rights. All three agreements run for only one season.

Mfor notes that the television-rights fee has fallen by 40% from the HUF 10 billion paid under the previous agreement. However, the additional Szerencsejáték funding means the amount available for redistribution to clubs has not fallen at the same rate.

Sports economist János Kele argued in the Mfor analysis that this funding structure weakens the immediate commercial incentive for clubs to maximise paying attendance. Supporters remain crucial for atmosphere, sponsorship appeal, community links and long-term brand value, he stressed, but their direct contribution at the turnstiles is relatively small.

Financial incentives can even affect team selection

The system also has a direct sporting dimension. Under the MLSZ rules, NB I clubs are encouraged financially to field Hungarian and young players. On average, five Hungarian players should be on the pitch, including one under-21 footballer.

As much as 45% of the NB I central distribution is linked to domestic and young-player minutes. On a HUF 10.5 billion central pool, that represents as much as HUF 4.725 billion (around EUR 13 million).

The incentive has already influenced decisions on the pitch. Mfor cited Nyíregyháza’s match against Újpest, when 19-year-old goalkeeper Mátyás Molnár came on at half-time. Head coach Tamás Bódog acknowledged afterwards that complying with the youth-player requirement was a factor in the substitution.

As we wrote earlier, Dominik Szoboszlai signs a new Liverpool deal until 2031, read details here

Ferencváros operates on a different scale

The financial differences between individual Hungarian clubs are also substantial. According to the G7-based calculations cited by Mfor, Ferencváros had a budget approaching HUF 20 billion (EUR 55 million) in 2024, while smaller provincial clubs typically operated with HUF 2–3 billion (roughly EUR 5.5–8.2 million).

Paks, for example, recorded HUF 2.9 billion (EUR 8 million) in revenue while finishing third in the league and winning the Hungarian Cup. Ferencváros, meanwhile, benefits not only from a much larger budget but also from European competition, a larger stadium, a stronger commercial brand and greater visibility on the international transfer market.

Player sales brought NB I clubs HUF 9.3 billion (EUR 25.6 million) in 2024, close to 15% of overall revenue. However, Mfor notes that the MLSZ’s own strategy identifies Hungary as having the lowest share of player-sale income among the regional leagues it studied, as well as a negative net transfer balance.

Billions invested, but few international youth successes

Hungary’s record in men’s youth football offers another perspective on the sums flowing into the domestic game. Since 2010, Hungarian teams have qualified for the finals of a men’s youth European Championship through the qualifiers on only a handful of occasions. The standout period came at U17 level: Hungary reached the 2017 U17 European Championship, its first appearance at that tournament since 2006, and qualified again for the 2019 edition. UEFA records confirm both appearances. The 2019 side went one step further, earning a place at the FIFA U17 World Cup in Brazil through its performance at the European Championship, UEFA said.

Other tournament appearances during this period need some context. Hungary played at the 2014 U19 European Championship as the host nation, and its result there secured qualification for the 2015 FIFA U20 World Cup. UEFA explicitly listed Hungary as the host rather than one of the seven teams that qualified through the elite round. Similarly, Hungary participated in the 2021 U21 European Championship as co-host with Slovenia, while the 2023 U17 European Championship was also staged in Hungary, giving the home team an automatic place.

In other words, despite the considerable resources channelled into Hungarian football, 2019 remains the last time a Hungarian men’s youth national team qualified for a European Championship through the qualifying competition – and also the last time one earned a place at a youth World Cup on the pitch.

Conclusion

The figures illustrate the central question facing Hungarian football finances: whether clubs can gradually build a model based more strongly on supporters, commercial income and profitable player development, or whether their financial stability will continue to depend primarily on centrally negotiated and distributed funding. With the main broadcasting, marketing and betting agreements currently guaranteed for only the 2026/27 season, that debate is likely to remain highly relevant beyond the current campaign.

It is, however, very disheartening that in recent years the clubs have made no effort to increase attendance figures or sell their own branded merchandise, as they have essentially been receiving funding from the central budget. If, however, revenue from the fund decreases, they will have to adopt models similar to those of the major European clubs, where clubs encourage supporters to purchase season tickets and match tickets, for example.

World.title: Russian Rosatom breaks silence as it builds Hungary’s newest nuclear reactors
World.content:
Russia’s Rosatom is accelerating work on the Paks II project, which will provide Hungary with two new nuclear reactors, but a key political relationship behind the massive investment has changed dramatically. While Viktor Orbán’s governments maintained unusually close ties with Moscow for years, Rosatom now says it has established working relations with the new management of the Hungarian project company – but has received no approach from Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government itself.

Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev discussed both the construction and the changed political environment in comments to the Russian press on Thursday. According to a statement by the Russian state nuclear corporation reported by MTI, construction at Paks has accelerated and Rosatom says it is proceeding according to the schedule agreed with its Hungarian client.

The distinction between cooperation with the project company and relations with the government is increasingly significant. Hungary changed governments in May after Péter Magyar defeated Viktor Orbán, ending 16 years of continuous Fidesz rule. The new administration has already announced that it intends to review both the financing and implementation of Paks II.

Rosatom: Magyar government has not approached us

Likhachev said the management of Paks II Nuclear Power Plant Ltd changed around a month ago and Rosatom had already established a working relationship with the new leadership.

Relations at government level appear to be another matter.

Rosatom is ready for dialogue and prepared to provide factual and quantifiable answers to any questions raised by the Hungarian government, Likhachev said. However, the company has so far received no approach from the new government.

That is a striking change from the political environment in which the Paks II project was created. Orbán’s government awarded the project to Russia’s state-owned Rosatom in 2014 without an open tender. Over the following years, Orbán maintained close political and energy ties with Moscow even as Hungary’s relations with several EU partners deteriorated.

After Orbán’s election defeat in April, Reuters described his departure as a significant change for Moscow, noting his close ties with Russia, his support for continued Russian energy imports and his opposition to several EU measures against Moscow. The Kremlin responded to Magyar’s victory by expressing hope for pragmatic relations with the new Hungarian leadership.

Magyar’s government has taken a different approach. Foreign Minister Anita Orbán has said Hungary’s primary alliances are the European Union and NATO and that Budapest wants an equal and transparent relationship with Russia. At the same time, the government has not proposed cutting all energy ties with Moscow. Reuters reported in May that the administration intended to review Paks II while diversifying Hungary’s energy sources.

As we wrote earlier, Putin’s people take aim at PM Magyar again, this time mocking the energy crisis and Paks

Paks II construction is meanwhile moving ahead

Political uncertainty has not stopped physical construction.

Likhachev said the foundation of the Unit 5 reactor building is now around 80% complete, with more than 18,000 cubic metres of concrete already poured. Rosatom expects the foundation to be completed before winter.

The first concrete for Unit 5 was poured on 5 February 2026, a milestone that means the new plant officially qualifies as being under construction according to International Atomic Energy Agency terminology, as confirmed by the official Paks II project company.

Work is also progressing on Unit 6, where excavation for the reactor building is under way. Preparations for its first concrete pour are expected to begin before the end of the year.

Rosatom has also started manufacturing reactor equipment for both units. Components of the Unit 5 reactor pressure vessel have been completed and assembly is expected to start shortly. Around 500 people are currently working at the Paks II construction site, according to Likhachev. Companies from Hungary, Russia, France, the United States, Germany, Austria, the Czech Republic and several other countries are involved in the project.

If you missed it: Horror over Paks II NPP overpricing: did Orbán-linked and Tisza-affiliated businessmen and politicians pocket the cash?

Magyar wants Paks II reviewed as Danube problems intensify

The political debate has become even more urgent because of Hungary’s recent energy problems.

Record-low water levels on the Danube forced the existing Paks nuclear plant to slash production earlier in August. Péter Magyar subsequently said that Paks II must be reconsidered from a cooling perspective as well, because the new reactors are currently also designed to rely on the Danube.

According to Reuters, Magyar said the project had already become significantly more expensive than originally planned and that its cooling system should be renegotiated, with alternatives such as cooling towers also considered.

The result is an unusual situation: Russia is already building Hungary’s next two nuclear reactors, while the political relationship that produced the deal has fundamentally changed.

Rosatom is signalling that it wants the Paks II project to continue without further delay. Magyar’s government, meanwhile, has promised to scrutinise the project, its financing and its dependence on the Danube. Whether Budapest and Moscow can establish the pragmatic relationship required to complete one of Hungary’s largest-ever infrastructure projects may now become just as important as the concrete being poured at Paks.

World.title: VIDEOS: Ferencváros fans attacked in Poland before Europa League clash, Hungarian supporter injured
World.content:
Ferencváros fans were attacked in Poland on Wednesday evening ahead of the Hungarian champions’ Europa League qualifier against Górnik Zabrze. A large group of masked attackers targeted a restaurant in the centre of Zabrze where Hungarian supporters were staying, leaving one Hungarian man with a broken leg. Police are working to identify those involved.

The incident took place on Wednesday, 12 August, just one day before Ferencváros were due to face Górnik Zabrze in the second leg of their UEFA Europa League third qualifying round tie.

A group associated with Górnik Zabrze supporters attacked Ferencváros fans at a pizzeria in the Polish city. The Hungarian supporters barricaded themselves inside after the attackers began throwing objects at the building and smashing its windows.

Up to 100 masked attackers reported in Zabrze

Polish broadcaster TVN24, which spoke directly to Zabrze police spokesman Sebastian Bijok, reported that police received the first call about the incident at 9.27 pm on Wednesday.

There were around a dozen people inside the restaurant, including Hungarian and Slovak nationals. Police said the attackers were masked, while some were wearing colours associated with Torcida, the best-known organised Górnik Zabrze supporter group, and were reportedly shouting slogans connected to the Polish club.

Initial witness accounts put the number of attackers at between 50 and 100, although police stressed that the figure remained uncertain and would have to be checked against CCTV footage. Officers from the local police force and a public-order unit from Katowice were sent to the scene, but the attackers dispersed before police arrived.

Grupa pseudokibiców zaatakowała gości pizzerii w centrum Zabrza. Jak podaje policja, zaatakowani to między innymi obywatele Węgier. Lokal został zdemolowany, co pokazuje nagranie z monitoringu. Na miejscu była reporterka TVN24 Małgorzata Marczok, która opowiedziała o szczegółach… pic.twitter.com/6r5rB6HkjW — tvn24 (@tvn24) August 13, 2026

Police also found empty containers from handheld gas sprays that had apparently been used during the confrontation, TVN24 reported. The restaurant itself suffered substantial damage.

If you missed it: Ferencváros narrowly beaten by Real Madrid in Budapest

Hungarian supporter suffers broken leg

One Hungarian man was injured during the incident. According to the account given to Polish police, he attempted to escape by jumping over a fence but landed badly and broke his leg. He was subsequently taken to a local hospital.

TVN24 reported that ten Hungarian nationals were questioned, but none had filed a formal criminal complaint at the time of the broadcaster’s report. No suspects had been detained, although police said they were analysing surveillance footage and working to establish the identities of those responsible.

Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán condemned the violence, according to Telex. She said Hungary’s Consulate General was maintaining continuous contact with the Zabrze police and both football clubs. She also said people suspected of involvement had been subjected to identity checks. Hungary’s official government website confirms Orbán as the country’s current foreign minister.

Ferencváros take a 1–0 advantage into the return leg

The attack comes just hours before an important European fixture for Hungary’s most successful football club.

According to UEFA, Górnik Zabrze and Ferencváros meet on Thursday, 13 August, in the second leg of the UEFA Europa League third qualifying round. Ferencváros hold a one-goal advantage after winning the first leg 1–0 in Budapest.

The Hungarian club’s official match report said Marius Corbu scored the only goal of the first encounter, giving Ferencváros the advantage ahead of the trip to Poland.

Górnik Zabrze’s official website likewise confirmed that the return match is scheduled for 7 pm local time at Arena Zabrze.

Telex reported that buses organised by Ferencváros for travelling supporters were expected to arrive at the stadium at around 5 pm on Thursday, where Hungary’s consul-general was due to meet them.

The investigation into Wednesday night’s violence is continuing. As of Thursday morning, Polish police had announced no arrests, while officers were examining CCTV footage in an effort to identify the masked attackers.

World.title: Weekend weather in Hungary: heatwave returns, temperatures may reach 37°C by Sunday
World.content:
The weekend weather in Hungary will bring the return of intense summer heat, with mostly cloudless skies, virtually no rain and temperatures climbing above 30°C across the country. The hottest conditions are expected on Sunday, when afternoon highs could reach 37°C, according to the latest forecast from HungaroMet, Hungary’s national meteorological service.

After a slight easing of the heat earlier in the week, temperatures will rise steadily from Friday, 14 August, through Sunday, 16 August. The dry spell will also continue, adding further pressure to areas already affected by severe agricultural drought. HungaroMet said earlier this week that most of Hungary was experiencing severe or extreme agricultural drought, with no meaningful rainfall expected in the days ahead.

Friday: sunny and dry across Hungary

Friday will be largely cloudless and sunny throughout the country. Some cumulus clouds may develop in eastern Hungary, but rainfall is not expected.

Winds will generally remain light or moderate and will come mainly from the east, although they could strengthen at times over the Northern Great Plain.

Daytime temperatures will already be high. HungaroMet’s latest national outlook indicates maximum temperatures of roughly 28–33°C, meaning summer heat will be felt almost everywhere.

Despite the rising temperatures, HungaroMet said no weather event meeting its official warning criteria was expected anywhere in Hungary up to midnight on Friday.

As we wrote today, the danger is not over, Budapest water supply under pressure again

Weekend weather in Hungary turns hotter on Saturday

Saturday will mark a more noticeable return of the heatwave. Mostly clear and dry weather is forecast, with only limited cloud development possible in eastern and south-eastern parts of Hungary.

Southerly winds may strengthen locally, while temperatures will show a considerable difference between the cool early morning and the hot afternoon.

Minimum temperatures are expected to range between 7°C and 20°C, with the lowest values likely in sheltered and traditionally cooler locations. By the afternoon, however, temperatures will rise to 30–35°C.

HungaroMet has also indicated first-level warnings for high daily mean temperatures in ten counties, including Pest, Bács-Kiskun, Békés, Csongrád-Csanád, Fejér, Győr-Moson-Sopron, Komárom-Esztergom, Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok, Tolna and Veszprém. In these areas, the daily average temperature may exceed 25°C.

For foreign visitors, this means that even if mornings remain relatively comfortable in some parts of the country, conditions can become significantly hotter by early afternoon. Travellers planning sightseeing, hiking or outdoor activities should therefore be prepared for strong summer heat.

Sunday could bring temperatures of up to 37°C

The hottest part of the weekend is expected on Sunday. Mostly clear and sunny conditions will continue, although some clouds could reach north-western Hungary. Rain remains unlikely, while southerly winds may become brisk in places.

Morning temperatures are expected to range from around 10°C to 22°C, before the air heats up rapidly during the day. According to HungaroMet’s current forecast, afternoon highs are likely to reach 33–37°C.

City forecasts also point to intense heat: around 36°C is currently expected in Budapest and Győr, while Szeged and Debrecen could reach approximately 35°C on Sunday.

Dry weather adds to Hungary’s drought problems

The lack of rain is becoming increasingly significant. HungaroMet’s agricultural assessment published on 10 August said that rainfall over the previous months had fallen well below the long-term average in much of Hungary, while soil moisture levels were critically low across large areas.

The weekend weather in Hungary will therefore be favourable for outdoor programmes in terms of sunshine and the low risk of rain, but the rapidly intensifying heat will become the main concern. By Sunday afternoon, much of the country is likely to experience genuine heatwave conditions, bringing another spell of very hot and exceptionally dry weather to Hungary.

World.title: WWF slams Hungarian government’s Danube underwater weir plan
World.content:
The underwater weir designed to ensure the cooling water supply for the Paks nuclear power station may offer a quick solution to the problem of low water levels but it is currently impossible to assess how this will resolve the decades-long deepening of the Danube’s riverbed, a WWF expert told MTI on Thursday.

Tamás Gruber (WWF) said that given the current, extremely low water levels, intervention aimed at raising the water level was to be expected. However, it is difficult to find an adequate solution in a short time for a complex problem that has persisted for decades, and there is not enough time for comprehensive planning, he added.

The underwater weir may be able to retain water and raise the water level on the upstream side, but on the downstream side it could further exacerbate the low-water situation, he said. It is important to continuously monitor the riverbed sections both upstream and downstream of the underwater weir, from both technical and ecological perspectives, he said.

If you missed it: the danger is not over, Budapest water supply is under pressure again

He said that any intervention affecting the Danube must simultaneously take into account energy generation, navigation, water management and ecological considerations.

He said there had already been examples of similar technical solutions on smaller rivers in Hungary, primarily on the Raba and in certain parts of the Szigetköz, but their size and technical design are not comparable to the current plans.

He warned that

the construction of the underwater weir did not mean that the current water shortage will be resolved, and added that the prudent use of energy and water will remain necessary in the coming months.
